title: What are you carrying?
goal: Mark the object of an action with the endings -am and -um, use the six forms of 1st-group verbs, and build complete subject-object-verb sentences.
bekal: turn a noun into its object form and know why it matters
say *I carry, you carry, we carry* with one pattern
build a correct three-word sentence without relying on word order

dialogs.title: Colloquium — Cena paratur
dialogs.intro: Evening at Quintus's house. Cornelia is getting dinner ready, and everyone is carrying something.

lines.speaker: Marcus:
lines.text: Aquam porto, mater. Aqua frigida est.
lines.id: I'm carrying water, Mom. The water is cold.
lines.literal: water-obj carry-I, mother-call. water cold-fem is-it.

lines.speaker: Cornelia:
lines.id: Good. And Iulia? What is she making?

lines.speaker: Marcus:
lines.text: Iulia cenam parat. Sed cantat quoque!
lines.id: Iulia is making dinner. But she's singing too!
lines.literal: Iulia dinner-obj prepare-she. but sing-she also!

lines.speaker: Cornelia:
lines.id: Iulia is always singing. Is she telling a story too?

lines.speaker: Marcus:
lines.text: Ita, fabulam longam narrat. Sextus fabulam laudat.
lines.id: Yes, a long one. Sextus is praising her story.
lines.literal: yes, story-obj long-obj tell-she. Sextus story-obj praise-he.

lines.speaker: Cornelia:
lines.text: Ubi est Sextus? Cur non laborat?
lines.id: Where's Sextus? Why isn't he working?
lines.literal: where is-he Sextus? why not work-he?

lines.speaker: Marcus:
lines.text: Sextus ambulat et cantat. Non laborat!
lines.id: Sextus is walking around and singing. He isn't working!
lines.literal: Sextus walk-he and sing-he. not work-he!

lines.speaker: Cornelia:
lines.id: I'll call Sextus. We're waiting for dinner!

lines.speaker: Marcus:
lines.text: Ego mensam porto. Iulia aquam portat.
lines.id: I'm carrying the table. Iulia is carrying the water.
lines.literal: I table-obj carry-I. Iulia water-obj carry-she.

lines.speaker: Cornelia:
lines.text: Bonus filius es, Marce. Te laudo.
lines.id: You're a good son, Marcus. I'm proud of you.
lines.literal: good-masc son-masc are-you, Marcus-call. you-obj praise-I.

lines.speaker: Marcus:
lines.id: Thanks, Mom! Now let's get dinner ready.

notes: **Aqua and aquam are two different things.** *Aqua frigida est* — "the water is cold"; here the water is the subject. *Aquam porto* — "I'm carrying water"; here the water is what the action is done to, and its ending changes to *-am*. This one-letter change does the job that word order does in English.

**Adjectives wear the object hat too.** Look at *fabulam longam*: because *fabulam* has the object ending, *longam* must follow. An adjective always wears exactly the same outfit as its noun — gender, number and job must all match.

**All the verbs in this dialogue follow one pattern.** *Porto, parat, narrat, laudat, laborat, ambulat, cantat, voco, exspectamus, paramus* — ten verbs, one pattern. This group is called the first conjugation, and it's the biggest and most regular in all of Latin.

**Te laudo — pronouns have an object form too.** *Ego* becomes *me*, *tu* becomes *te* — just like English *I/me*. So *te laudo* means "I praise you" and *me laudas* means "you praise me". You can swap the order without changing the meaning, because the endings do the work.

sections.title: The object form: the -am and -um hat

blocks.text: When a noun is the object of an action — the thing carried, seen or called — it takes a special form. In grammar books it's called the accusative; in this course it's marked `-obj` in the literal line.

Look at the last rows: neuter words **don't change at all**. *Templum* is both subject and object, and only the sentence tells you which is meant. This rule holds in all five declensions without exception — neuter words always have twin subject and object forms.

blocks.title: Why this is such a powerful tool
items: *Puella puerum vocat* and *Puerum puella vocat* mean the same: the girl calls the boy. The endings already say who does what, so word order is free to be used for emphasis.
*Puellam puer vocat* means the opposite, even though the words are the same. Read the endings first, not the order.
So when reading a Latin sentence, get into the habit of looking for the object ending first. It almost always attaches to the verb.

blocks.text: A Latin verb's dictionary form starts with the "I" form: *porto, portare* — "I carry, to carry". If the second form ends in *-are*, the verb belongs to the first group, and you can build all its forms yourself. Here's how: drop the *-re* from *portare*, leaving *porta-*, then attach the six person endings.

Those six endings — *-o, -s, -t, -mus, -tis, -nt* — are the person endings for **all** Latin verbs, in every group, in almost every tense. You've just learned a third of the whole Latin verb system. The only thing that differs between groups is the linking vowel before the ending.
Notice that the "I" form swallows the *a*: not *portao* but *porto*. That's the only quirk in the first group, and it applies to all of them: *amo*, *voco*, *laboro*, *specto*.

blocks.text: The subject slot can stay empty, because the verb ending already names it. The object slot can stay empty too if the action isn't done to anything: *Sextus ambulat* — "Sextus walks".
